content: The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes that products intended for use in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) must meet specific criteria for programmatic suitability and be prequalified by WHO. This prequalification process serves as an international benchmark for ensuring the quality, safety, efficacy, and suitability of products for public health programs in LMICs. Developers and manufacturers are encouraged to engage with the WHO prequalification team early in the development process to discuss product specifications and regulatory requirements. Access to biotherapeutic products, including biosimilars, is critical for addressing public health needs. WHO has urged member states to strengthen their national regulatory assessment capacities to facilitate the availability of these products. Recognizing the challenges many countries face in regulating monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), WHO has published guidance documents on regulatory considerations for biotherapeutics and mAbs as biosimilar products. In 2019, WHO launched a pilot project to prequalify select biosimilars, resulting in the prequalification of the first trastuzumab biosimilar for breast and stomach cancer treatment. Preferred product characteristics (PPCs) for mAbs used in HIV prevention have been outlined. These mAbs are intended for the prevention of HIV-1 infection in confirmed HIV-negative individuals. They should not be used in HIV-infected pregnant women to avoid the selection and transfer of resistant viruses to infants. Target populations include individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection, such as men who have sex with men (MSM), sex workers, people who inject drugs (PWID), transgender individuals, and people in prisons or closed settings. Other groups include adolescents, cisgender men and women in high-prevalence settings, pregnant and breastfeeding women, neonates, and infants with HIV exposure, as well as serodiscordant couples. Key populations and their sexual partners account for over 65% of new HIV infections globally, making them a critical focus for prevention efforts. Adolescent girls and young women in sub-Saharan Africa, the epicenter of the HIV epidemic, are particularly prioritized. Prevention products suitable for use during conception, pregnancy, and breastfeeding are essential. Given the long half-life of mAbs, they may be effective in preventing vertical transmission of HIV. Cost-effectiveness, acceptability, and broad availability of mAbs are important considerations. Manufacturers should ensure that intellectual property filings, out-licensing, and pricing do not hinder global access. Products should be made widely available, especially in high-burden countries and populations that participate in clinical development. Delivery strategies should align with existing health programs, such as those for preventing vertical transmission or vaccine delivery infrastructure. Safety is a critical aspect of mAb development. These products should have a favorable safety profile and be safe for use in pregnancy, breastfeeding, older adolescents, and infants. Clinical trials have shown that single and repeated administrations of anti-HIV-1 mAb combinations are generally well-tolerated, with infrequent adverse events reported. WHO specifies that intravenous (IV) administration is not broadly suitable for programmatic implementation in LMICs due to logistical challenges. Subcutaneous administration is preferred, and efforts are underway to increase the injectable volume for this route. Fixed, non-weight-based dosing with age-appropriate adjustments is recommended to simplify administration and accommodate growth. Product stability and storage are also critical. mAbs should ideally be stable under refrigerated conditions (2–8°C) for 2–3 years. Room-temperature, lyophilized formulations may be preferable, but technical and implementation considerations, such as ready-to-use formats, must be factored into formulation decisions. WHO prequalification is often used as a reliance mechanism to support licensure in LMICs and enable procurement through UN agencies and other global mechanisms. Close collaboration with WHO and national regulatory authorities is essential to ensure programmatic implementation and adherence. Sustained protection with repeated use should be evaluated through long-term follow-up studies and post-introduction surveillance. Finally, the development of mAbs for HIV prevention should consider the genetic diversity of HIV-1 across geographies and populations. Trial designs should conform to regulatory standards and ethical considerations, ensuring access to a package of recommended prevention methods. Developers should aim to demonstrate non-inferiority or superiority to current standards of care, while addressing logistical and cost barriers.
